Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: Art Institute of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA - Museum Tour
Tour-Category: museum

Stop 1: The Great Wave of Kanagawa

Coordinates: 41.8781, -87.6298

Museum Information:

The museum is open daily except Tuesday, 11:00 to 5:00. Admission is 25 dollars for adults; under-14s go free.

Orientation: You are about to explore the Art Institute of Chicago in Chicago. These diverse pieces span different periods and cultures, yet collectively offer a profound exploration of human experience. Your first stop is The Great Wave of Kanagawa. Stand close enough that you can see the subtle emboss of the paper’s edge and the fine layering of color—details that reveal this is not a painting but a woodblock print. From here, the shifting blue of the waves and the distant, almost ghostlike Mount Fuji come into focus, revealing Hokusai’s sense of movement and scale in a way that dissolves when viewed at a distance.

Katsushika Hokusai, the Japanese ukiyo-e artist, designed The Great Wave of Kanagawa in Edo, now called Tokyo. In late 1831, Hokusai created this woodblock print as part of his Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji series, making each image with a combination of carved wood blocks and layered, mineral-based pigments. Hokusai produced thousands of impressions of this design, ensuring that the Great Wave circulated throughout Japan and far beyond in subsequent generations. Over time, Hokusai’s work traveled across continents, eventually reaching the Art Institute of Chicago. However, because the print’s organic and mineral pigments are highly sensitive to light, the museum decided to keep these prints in climate-controlled vault storage. This means Hokusai’s Great Wave is shown only during brief, carefully timed rotations, and only a fraction of visitors ever view the original in person, preserving its color and detail for the future. The print itself measures about 25.7 by 37.9 centimeters, its landscape format—known in Japanese as yoko-e—allowing Hokusai to stretch the form of the wave nearly to the edge of the paper. Foreground boats buckle and tilt beneath a crest curling like a giant claw, while Mount Fuji remains steady and small in the distance, almost swallowed by water and spray. Hokusai, in his seventies when he made this, had survived personal hardship and was reaching for something enduring: a moment when nature’s force both dwarfs and defines humanity’s efforts. The awe in the work is palpable—the sense of one world crashing against another, and of humanity’s smallness within it. This feeling lingers, echoing in cities around the world, wherever people gather beneath something vast and uncontrollable.

Directions: Continue through Art Institute of Chicago — next is Paris Street; Rainy Day.

Stop 2: Paris Street; Rainy Day

Coordinates: 41.8781, -87.6298

Orientation: Least ten feet back from Paris Street; Rainy Day is directly in front of its lower left corner, where the date “1877” and Gustave Caillebotte’s signature anchor the scene in time. From this vantage point, the full breadth of the canvas—over seven feet tall—unfolds, allowing the vertical streetlamp that bisects the painting to dominate your field of vision. The lamplight’s sharp division clarifies how Caillebotte structured his streetscape: figures on either side seem to move in and out of shadow, and the scale of the composition envelops the viewer, evoking the sensation of standing amid the damp Parisian boulevard.

The painting’s surface is oil on canvas—its physical weight and monumental size giving each figure the presence of life-size passersby. The careful rendering of wet cobblestones and the sheen on umbrellas signals the artist’s command of paint to suggest atmosphere. In 1877, Caillebotte found himself at a turning point, merging the precision of architectural drafts with the Impressionists’ passion for city life. Unlike the cresting force of The Great Wave of Kanagawa, which you viewed earlier, this painting dwells in the moment after the storm—when the city resumes, and movement continues under glistening skies. In its scale and construction, Paris Street; Rainy Day captures the quiet drama of individuals set against the machinery of modern urban space, raising the question of what changes when such perspective and scale are carried to the open air and shifting light of rural America.

Your final stop in Art Institute of Chicago: American Gothic.

Stop 3: American Gothic by Grant Wood

Coordinates: 41.8781, -87.6298

Orientation: As you stand here, let your gaze settle on "American Gothic" by Grant Wood—move a few steps back, centering yourself so you see both the stern faces and the precise verticals of the farmhouse window above them. This position reveals how the composition draws the eye between the figures and the sharp geometry of the background, a contrast easy to miss up close.

Grant Wood painted "American Gothic" in oil on beaverboard, an inexpensive yet sturdy material that suited both his circumstances and the subject matter. The painting depicts a Midwestern farmer and his daughter, posed for by Wood’s sister, Nan Wood Graham, and his dentist. They stand rigidly before a white house with a pointed Gothic window—a detail Wood noticed while traveling through Eldon, Iowa, and selected for its out-of-place elegance. Nan Wood Graham posed for the daughter figure in Cedar Rapids, allowing Wood to compose the now-iconic pose.

From this viewing distance, you can see the deliberate care in the brushstrokes—crisp lines, flat areas of color, and the uncanny clarity of each feature. Here, the quiet intensity, the compressed space between the figures, and the almost airless stillness convey a particular experience of rural American life during a time of national uncertainty.

That same year, Wood, then mostly unknown outside Iowa, decided to send this painting to the Art Institute’s juried annual open exhibition. Grant Wood’s "American Gothic" endures in this gallery, a witness to transformative moments for the artist, for the museum, and for the way American identity is pictured.

This tour explores the interplay between nature and urban life, as well as the resilience of the human spirit in the face of uncertainty. These themes resonate through works like "American Gothic," inviting us to reflect on our own experiences within the broader tapestry of society.

That's 3 stops in all.
